With the number of available grants remaining fixed, the surge in submissions is driving the success rates sharply lower and rendering the system unsustainable, experts told Trouw. For example, for the European Research Council’s 2027 Starting Grant, 7,710 early-career scientists applied. Only 373 will receive funding, dropping the success rate below five percent. The EU’s Marie Curie program saw 21,627 submissions this year - nearly 27 percent more than last year. At the Dutch NWO, a spokesperson told Trouw that the success rate of getting a grant is falling. “We aim for an award rate of 20 to 25 percent, because otherwise too many scientists are busy in vain with such a time-consuming application. But we will probably soon have to announce that for one grant the success rate has fallen below 10 percent.” The spokesperson did not say which specific program that concerns. Serge Horbach, a researcher at Radbound University who studies the scientific system, says this is partly due to the rise of artificial intelligence. In recent years, scientific journals and conferences have reportedly been flooded with submissions that have been written entirely or partly with AI. Something similar is now happening with research grants. “We also see such an increase at FWP,” Horbach said. He regularly assesses applications for this Flemish provider of scientific grants. “And the applications are of a different caliber than before. In the past you still came across submissions in which insufficient attention had been paid to content or language use. Those were easy to filter out. Now almost everything is tight and polished.” However, that polished look often falls apart under scrutiny. “As soon as we invite researchers for an interview, some of them fall rather short,” Horbach said. “They cannot properly explain how they intend to carry out their research. By then they have already taken an interview slot that should have gone to a stronger candidate.”
